Westrand Zama Violence

By: Graham Coetzer | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
The harsh legacy of mining gone wrong as we meet the small community of West Village where running gunbattles between rival zama groups have residents living like prisoners in their own homes

Unique Selling Point:
The liquidation of the massive Mintails gold mining group's operations in and around Krugersdorp and Randfontein has caused what has been called one of South Africa's worst environmental catastrophes. But a darker, more dangerous part of that legacy is once again causing havoc for communities living in the wake of the Mintails disaster - with the mine abandoned and unprotected by private security, and the SAPS unwilling to act as a security force, the land was overrun by large groups of artisanal miners, the Zama zamas. As their turf wars for control of the lucrative minerals heat up, innocent communities are caught in the cross fire.

Summary:
The people living in West Village - a once affluent development of residential homes built by the Mintails group, are literally surrounded by abandoned mining land on all sides. And as gunfights between rival zama gangs erupt, they are often caught in the middle. Many zamas, often openly armed with AK 47's and the like, walk through the village to cross between mining sites. Residents say shootings are a weekly occurrence, with bullets flying through gardens as children play. Police are often slow to respond to cries of help, if at all. Residents say their homes have lost all value, and as the sun sets each evening, they lock the doors and hide in their houses.

Further information:
- We have secured an interview with a group of zamas who are mining in the area.
- We are taking two armed security with us for when we enter the zama areas.
- The whole area is dangerous, and we will take as much precaution as possible
- We have a drone for aerials.
- We have previous footage of police raids in the area.
- We have voice notes of residents calling for help/in fear on their community whatsapp group.
- We have case studies from residents and Zamas
- We will speak to the Legal Resources Centre to get the history and ongoing court battles around the liquidation and environmental liabilities.

Press Release:


I N V E S T I G A T I O N S



Zama Wars in the Wild West

On Johannesburg’s West Rand, over 1700 hectares of waste piles and open pits have been left behind after the 2018 liquidation of the Australian company Mintails Mining South Africa. With an ongoing legal battle relating to a multi-million environmental liability claim, the land lies abandoned and unsecured. Now overrun by gangs of illegal miners fighting for a share in the lucrative gold remnants still in the ground, Carte Blanche meets the communities caught in the crossfire and examines whether formalising artisanal mining could provide a way forward.

Producer: Graham Coetzer | Presenter: Macfarlane Moleli

Watch the trailer

Script:


Westrand Zama Violence
7 June 2021
Forst Draft Script


Sound Up Whatsapp voice notes


Please get inside your houses, shots fired in the village, please get back in your houses
Please, please people, we need help! They are waiting at our windows for us. Please we need help.
we found the bullet in the yard, they shot here as well.

Voice
What you’ve just heard are whatsapp voice notes sent to us by terrified residents of a once prosperous mining village just outside of Krugersdorp.

Link Mac
This is West Village - a small community who live in residential houses that used to belong to the mine. But the Village’s glory days are long gone - and homeowners here say that once the sun sets, they lock themselves inside their houses in absolute fear.

Voice
The sprawling 1700 hectares of waste piles and open pits, which surround West Village, used to be a rich source of gold for Mintails Mining South Africa. But in 2018, the company was placed into final liquidation. Since it’s collapse Mintails has been embroiled in litigation around an unfunded environmental liability that runs into the hundreds of millions of rands.

Steven Ndlovu has lived in West Village for more than a decade, but in recent years he says the crime situation has gotten so bad, he’s now letting his children live with family in Pretoria. And he blames the violence on the notorious illegal miners known as zama-zamas.

Sound Up Steven Ndlovu
Mac: And how was it before, how would you describe this place?

Steven: This was a nice place. Though there were shacks on that side by Makulugama, but there were no problems of these zama-zama people. There were zama-zamas, but there were not troubles like now. There’s a big trouble now, because of them, they are the trouble makers.

Voice
As Mintails imploded, the gold rich land was overrun by zamas, men willing to risk their lives to enter abandoned mining shafts in search of valuable minerals. In 2019 we accompanied police during a tense stand off with an armed group of zamas on the Mintails Mogale Gold Plant after it had been looted by hundreds of illegal miners.

Sound Up Derek Watts
The police say the zamas are still up on the hill, we’re going to go with them in this Casspir, and just see what develops.

Voice
Fast forward to 2021 and the zama problem has escalated, with experts estimating there are literally thousands of zamas now working the old Mintails properties. Shafts like this one, rich in ore, are hotly contested and gun battles between rival factions of zamas are an all too regular occurrence. Stuck right in the middle of it all, the residents of West Village.

Sound Up Steven
Steven: It’s dangerous, like before you arrive here, about 10-15 minutes before you came, there were two or three gunshots not far away from here.

Mac: Is this a daily occurrence?

Steven: As I’m telling you now, other day they were shooting in this road, in front of my house, one bullet hit the roof here.

Voice
And bullet riddled bodies are often found littering the streets.

Sound Up Steven
So about two months back somebody was shot behind my house, dead.

Voice
This leaked footage shows an attack on a gold processing facility just a few kilometers down the road. A large group of zamas shot one security guard, while others were held at gunpoint and badly beaten. Village resident Gideon Visagie says they’ve also had terrifying run-ins with the zama zamas.

Sound Up Gideon Visagie
My son was walking his dog, and he was on his way back home, and four of them started to chase him, and he ran into the yard. And four of them followed him into the property. They shot one of our dogs, and the bullet is still inside the dog.

Voice
Spiere, the family’s beloved mongrel, has since recovered but both he and the Visagies have been left traumatised by the events. Especially when they hear the all too familiar sound of gunshots at night.

Sound Up Gideon
Everybody in the house is very very scared. Sometimes, my daughter and my boys are sleeping with us in the room. It depends on how the shots are going.

Voice
Through careful negotiation, we were allowed access to a group of zamas who operate about a five minute drive from West Village. We found a uniquely South African situation - the zamas were mining right beside a licensed mining operation. The miners and the zamas here have an agreement to stay out of each other’s way. The illegal miners we met were were willing to speak to as long as we didn’t use their real names.

Sound Up “Adam”
02:18 (2:55)
Macfarlane: and then let’s say you worked well right , how much money do you make, how much gold can you take out in a day or a week or even a month?
02:32
Adam: it depends; you can find that this week you can get a one gram or two grams

02:36
Mac: yes
02:37
Adam: it’s not a sure thing
02:39
Mac: but one gram requires a lot of work to find?
02:41
Adam: yes, it’s a lot of work to find it
02:44
Mac: and then for that one gram, how much do you get when you go and sell it how much do you sell it for? How much is it on the market?
02:49
Adam: at 450
02:51
Mac: you sell it for R450?
02:52
Adam: yes.
Voice
That means a kilogram of zama gold is worth R450 000. And those prices have attracted organised crime syndicates. Heavily armed gangs often take over whole groups of zamas, and force them to work for the syndicates under threat of violence. The zamas say that’s what’s causing the crime on the streets of West Village.

Sound Up Adam
It’s the people that attack us and they really do shoot at us.
Voice
Even in licensed mines like this one, conditions underground are treacherous. But workers here have the benefits of health and safety protocols, and structural engineers who constantly monitor the tunnels for any signs of a cave in.

Link Mac
So this is a legal mining operation, and it’s quite safe. Well, that’s what they say. We’re using our own light so that we can see where we are going, I cannot even imagine what it must be like with the lights turned off, and you don’t even know where you are going.

Voice
The underground world the zamas inhabit is a dirty, dangerous place, with no support beams or other safety measures in sight. The men will often spend weeks underground, eating and drinking only the food they can carry with them, and performing backbreaking labour in search of illusive gold deposits.

Link Mac
As you can see it’s very informal, and the guys use their own ways and means to break the rock down, and hopefully this is where all the gold is.

Voice
Security expert Louis Nel has consulted with some of South Africa’s biggest mines on the illegal mining problem. He says the situation on the West Rand has gotten out of control.

Sound Up Louis
It can go up to 200 per group, fighting with semi-automatic weapons and everything. It’s very violent, and they take no prisoners. The strongest survive, that’s the rule. It’s managed and run by the illegal miners at this stage.

Voice
Nel says ordinary policemen are simply not equipped to deal with the problem.

Sound Up Louis
Mac: So it’s almost become like a no man’s land, is it easy for police to come in here?

Louis: No. If you just take a normal policeman from the Randfontein police station. He arrives here in a Nissan NP200 bakkie. They have to attend to a fight between rival groups - they are using high velocity weapons, semi-automatic weapons, it’s just not going to happen.

Voice
And even when police do bring in the big guns, finding and arresting armed groups of zamas in pitch darkness, in terrain the zamas know like the backs of their own hands, is an uphill battle.

Sound Up Derek Watts
What we are seeing is just how difficult it is for the police, it’s a lethal game of cat and mouse. The zamas can be anywhere, in the bushes, in the mine shafts, in this equipment, its really a thankless task.

Voice
So could formalising the industry get rid of the violence?

Link Mac
There’s always two sides to a story, and illegal mining is a complex social issue. So we’ve travelled to the North West province to the National Association of Artisanal Miners, not zama-zamas.

Voice
Chairperson Shawn Lethoko says the artisanal miners his association represents have formalised themselves into cooperatives, and are lobbying government to allow small scale operations like this one to be de-criminalised and licensed. He believes the move would take away the leverage criminal gangs have over his members.

Sound Up Shawn
It is operated by the cartels, yes these people you will find that behind them there is a rich person who has a lot of money, who is sponsoring them and then who is giving them this ammunition.

Voice
A day’s hard labour for these men might not even produce a single gram of gold - and they’ll have to split their earnings. Lethoko says because the work is still classified as illegal, they can’t complain to the police when the syndicates arrive.

Sound Up Shawn
And then when they get here, they will sometimes take us hostage, and then we will just have to work for them under their terms and conditions.

Voice
On the 5th of May this year, government released a draft policy that aims to formalise the illegal mining sector. Attorney Lauren Nel from the Legal Resources Centre, an organisation dedicated to improving human rights through use of the law, says they welcome the move.

Sound Up Lauren Nel
It is something we consider to be an achievement. The policy looks at different aspects of artisanal mining. From what the definitions are for artisanal mining vs small scale mining, what the licensing regime will look like. What’s very nice about it is that they obviously look at artisanal mining defined areas being set up.

Voice
But residents of West Village, like Steven Ndlovu, would like to see government take much stronger action to sort out the problem.

Sound Up Steven
Why don’t they give us like SANDF, to have a camp here for maybe two or three months, to control the situation.

This is West Village, when the sun sets here residents cower in fear from ongoing gun battles between illegal miners.

Sound Up Whatsapp message
shots fired in the village, please get back in your houses


Promo 2
In West Village near Krugersdorp, residents are caught in the crossfire as rival zama gangs wage deadly turf wars.

Sound Up Whatsapp message
Please, please people they are waiting at our windows for us, please we need help.


Promo 3
We meet the terrified residents of a Krugerdorp community who live in fear of the violence and bloodshed caused by roving gangs of the notorious zama zamas.

Sound Up Lauren Nel It is something we consider to be an achievement. The policy looks at different aspects of artisanal mining. From what the definitions are for artisanal mining vs small scale mining, what the licensing regime will look like. What’s very nice about it is that they obviously look at artisanal mining defined areas being set up. Voice But residents of West Village, like Steven Ndlovu, would like to see government take much stronger action to sort out the problem. Sound Up Steven Why don’t they give us like SANDF, to have a camp here for maybe two or three months, to control the situation. metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): The harsh legacy of mining gone wrong as we meet the small community of West Village where running gunbattles between rival zama groups have residents living like prisoners in their own homes
metadata.Unique Selling Point: The liquidation of the massive Mintails gold mining group's operations in and around Krugersdorp and Randfontein has caused what has been called one of South Africa's worst environmental catastrophes. But a darker, more dangerous part of that legacy is once again causing havoc for communities living in the wake of the Mintails disaster - with the mine abandoned and unprotected by private security, and the SAPS unwilling to act as a security force, the land was overrun by large groups of artisanal miners, the Zama zamas. As their turf wars for control of the lucrative minerals heat up, innocent communities are caught in the cross fire.
metadata.Summary: The people living in West Village - a once affluent development of residential homes built by the Mintails group, are literally surrounded by abandoned mining land on all sides. And as gunfights between rival zama gangs erupt, they are often caught in the middle. Many zamas, often openly armed with AK 47's and the like, walk through the village to cross between mining sites. Residents say shootings are a weekly occurrence, with bullets flying through gardens as children play. Police are often slow to respond to cries of help, if at all. Residents say their homes have lost all value, and as the sun sets each evening, they lock the doors and hide in their houses.
